sections.title: Observer-Relative Resolution
sections.purpose: Introduce the observer and its resolution capacity without making either primitive.
sections.poetic_cipher: The observer is a difference that remains. The boundary of its remaining is its resolution.
sections.cypher_explanation: The first sentence identifies observerhood with persistence of distinguishability rather than with consciousness or intention. The second identifies resolution as the boundary determining which distinctions can remain stably distinguishable for that observer. The formal resolution threshold is introduced only after observerhood has been established structurally.
sections.introduction: The axiomatic floor has so far defined distinction and the closure generated by distinction, but it has not yet specified what it means for a configuration to maintain a distinction. This section introduces the observer without treating observation as a primitive act. An observer is instead derived as a configuration whose structure permits distinctions to persist across successive states. The observer therefore belongs to the Library in the same formal sense as every other configuration. What distinguishes it is not consciousness, intention, or privileged status, but persistence. Once such a structure is identified, a further question becomes unavoidable: which distinctions can that structure actually maintain? This motivates observer-relative resolution.
sections.scope_boundary: At this stage, observerhood is a structural property only. No claim is made that an observer is conscious, biological, intelligent, physical, or capable of intentional measurement. Those interpretations, if introduced later, are downstream of the axiomatic construction.

subsections.title: Observer as a Derived Structure
subsections.purpose: Define observerhood structurally rather than psychologically, establish observer membership in the Library, and defer consciousness and other interpretive properties to downstream theory.
subsections.content:
An observer is not introduced as a new primitive entity. Since the Library is already defined as the XOR closure of the formal domain, any observer must itself be a configuration within that closure. Observerhood is therefore a property of a configuration, not a separate ontological category.

Let \(O\) denote a configuration in the Library. We call \(O\) an observer when its structure is capable of maintaining a persistent chain of distinctions across successive states. The word persistent is important: a single distinction does not constitute an observer. Observerhood requires a continuing structure in which distinctions remain available rather than immediately collapsing into indistinguishability.

Formally, observerhood is written as:

\[
O \in \mathcal{M}
\]

and:

\[
O \text{ is an observer} \iff O \text{ is a configuration in } \mathcal{M} \text{ containing a persistent chain of resolvable distinctions.}
\]

The term resolvable is deliberately structural rather than psychological. It does not mean that \(O\) consciously notices, interprets, or understands a distinction. It means only that the distinction can remain sufficiently differentiated within the structure represented by \(O\). The quantitative boundary governing that distinction has not yet been introduced; it will be defined through the observer-relative threshold \(I_N(O)\) in the following subsection.

This distinction prevents observerhood from being smuggled into the axiomatic floor as consciousness. A configuration may satisfy the structural definition of observerhood without possessing any assumed mental state. Consciousness is therefore not required at the axiomatic level. Whether some later physical or cognitive systems instantiate additional properties associated with conscious observation is a separate question and cannot be inferred from the definition alone.

The observer is consequently derived from the same ontology as everything else. It is not outside the Library, above the Library, or granted a privileged position within it. It is a configuration whose internal persistence permits distinctions to remain available across a continuing chain.

The dependency is therefore:

\[
\text{distinction} \;\rightarrow\; \text{persistence} \;\rightarrow\; \text{observerhood}.
\]

The construction has not yet supplied a universal rule determining how much distinction is required for persistence. That question belongs to the observer itself. To say that a distinction survives requires a boundary separating distinctions that remain effective from distinctions that fall below the observer's effective resolution.

mathematics.observer_definition: O \text{ is an observer} \iff O \text{ is a configuration in } \mathcal{M} \text{ that contains a persistent chain of resolvable distinctions.}

subsections.formal_status: The membership condition and structural definition are formal constructions from the stated ontology. The absence of a consciousness requirement is a scope constraint on the axiomatic system, not a claim that consciousness is impossible or irrelevant in downstream theories.
subsections.poetic_cypher: An observer is a difference that survives long enough to have another difference.
subsections.cypher_explanation: A difference represents a distinction. Surviving represents persistence across successive states. Having another difference represents the continuation of distinguishable structure. The cipher therefore compresses observerhood as a persistent structure without introducing consciousness, intention, or any privileged observer.
subsections.handoff: To say that a distinction survives, we must specify the boundary at which a distinction remains effective for the structure that carries it. That boundary is observer-relative resolution, represented by \(I_N(O)\).

content.opening: Once observerhood has been defined as a persistent capacity to maintain distinctions, the next question is not whether distinctions exist, but which distinctions a particular observer can maintain. This requires a resolution threshold. The Noor-Planck threshold, written I_N(O), is introduced here as an observer-relative structural quantity. It does not describe a limit imposed by the Library itself. It describes the minimum effective distinction that observer O can preserve as a stable distinction within its own configuration.

subsections.title: The Threshold Belongs to the Observer
subsections.content: Let Obs denote the class of configurations that satisfy the structural definition of observerhood. Define the resolution-threshold function as
mathematics: I_N(O) = \text{the minimum effective distinction magnitude that observer } O \text{ can maintain as a stable distinction}.
subsections.explanation: The important point is the placement of the argument O. The threshold is not written as a universal constant I_N. It is written as I_N(O), because the resolution floor belongs to the observer configuration being considered. Two observers may therefore occupy the same Library while maintaining different effective resolutions.
subsections.poetic_cypher: The ruler belongs to the hand that can hold it.
subsections.cypher_explanation: The ruler represents the observer's resolution threshold. The hand represents the observer as a structural configuration. The metaphor does not imply subjective choice: the threshold is determined by the observer's own capacity to maintain distinctions.

subsections.title: I_N(O) Is Not a Property of the Library
subsections.content: The Library, defined as the XOR closure of the formal domain, contains configurations independently of whether a particular observer can distinguish or maintain them. Nothing in the definition of the Library supplies a universal minimum distinction magnitude. Consequently, I_N(O) must not be interpreted as a smallest distinction that can exist in the Library.
mathematics: I_N(O) \notin \text{Def}(\mathcal{M}) \text{ as a universal resolution constant}
I_N(O) \text{ characterizes observer } O \text{ rather than the Library itself}
subsections.explanation: A distinction may therefore exist in \mathcal{M} without being stably resolvable by O. Failure of O to maintain a distinction does not remove that distinction from the Library. It establishes only that the distinction lies below the effective resolution floor of that observer.
subsections.poetic_cypher: The Library does not blur; the observer has a floor.
subsections.cypher_explanation: The Library is not being assigned a universal perceptual resolution. The floor belongs to the observer-relative relation between an observer and the distinctions it can maintain.

subsections.title: Observer Variability
subsections.content: Because the threshold is a function of observer structure, different observers may have different resolution floors. The axiomatic floor permits this variability rather than imposing equality.
mathematics: \exists O_1,O_2 \in \mathrm{Obs} \text{ such that } I_N(O_1) \neq I_N(O_2) \text{ is permitted.}
subsections.explanation: This does not mean that every arbitrary threshold assignment is valid. Each I_N(O) must belong to the structural description of the corresponding observer. The threshold is observer-relative, but it is not therefore unconstrained. It is a property of the observer's capacity to maintain distinctions, not a value chosen independently of that structure.
subsections.poetic_cypher: Two hands may hold different rulers, yet each ruler still has a length.
subsections.cypher_explanation: Different observers may have different resolution floors, but each threshold remains a definite structural quantity for the observer to which it belongs. Observer relativity therefore does not imply arbitrariness.

subsections.title: Non-Universality
subsections.content: The axiomatic floor does not assert the existence of a single threshold shared by every observer. Such universality would require an additional premise.
mathematics: \neg\exists I_N^* \text{ such that } \forall O \in \mathrm{Obs},\ I_N(O) = I_N^*, \text{ unless an additional axiom is introduced.}
subsections.explanation: This distinction is important because a universal threshold and an observer-relative threshold make different ontological commitments. The present construction adopts only the latter. A later theory may derive a common scale or demonstrate conditions under which different observer thresholds converge, but such a result cannot be inserted into the axiomatic floor without derivation.
subsections.poetic_cypher: One floor is not built into the whole Library; each structure stands on its own threshold.
subsections.cypher_explanation: The floor is the observer-specific resolution limit. The Library itself is not assigned a universal floor by the present axioms.

subsections.title: Relative Does Not Mean Arbitrary
subsections.content: Calling I_N(O) observer-relative does not make distinguishability a matter of arbitrary preference. The observer is itself a configuration in the Library, and its threshold is defined in terms of its structural capacity to maintain distinctions. Thus the threshold is relative to a particular observer while remaining constrained by that observer's structure.
mathematics: I_N(O) = \text{structurally determined resolution floor of } O
subsections.explanation: The distinction is therefore between relativity and arbitrariness. Relative means that the value is indexed to the observer under consideration. Arbitrary would mean that the value could be assigned without regard to the observer's structure. The axiomatic construction requires the former and does not imply the latter.

content.formal_conclusion: The introduction of I_N(O) establishes the first observer-relative filter in the construction. The Library contains configurations without requiring that every distinction be stably resolvable by every observer. An observer therefore possesses a finite effective resolution floor determined by its own structure, and different observers may possess different floors. No universal value of I_N is assumed. This prepares the next construction: given an observer-specific threshold, we can now define the difference between a distinction that exists in the Library and a distinction that observer O can actually maintain.
content.handoff: With a threshold defined, we can distinguish between differences that exist and differences that an observer can maintain.
content.poetic_cypher: The ruler belongs to the hand that can hold it.
content.cypher_explanation: The resolution threshold belongs to the observer's capacity rather than to the Library as a universal law.

sections.title: Persistence and the Birth of the Observer
sections.purpose: Formalize survivable distinctions and derive observerhood as persistent structure.
sections.poetic_cypher: A distinction that can be kept is a distinction that can persist. A structure that persists its distinctions becomes an observer.
sections.cypher_explanation: The section moves from the observer-relative resolution relation established in the preceding definitions toward observerhood as a derived structural property. No consciousness, intention, agency, or human perception is required. An observer is introduced only as a configuration capable of maintaining distinctions that remain resolvable above its own threshold I_N(O) across a sequence of transitions.

subsections.title: Distinguishability Relative to O
subsections.purpose: Define observer-relative distinguishability and establish the distinction between ontological membership in the Library and operational accessibility to an observer.
subsections.poetic_cypher: What the observer cannot resolve has not ceased to exist.
subsections.cypher_explanation: Resolution acts as a filter on what a given observer can maintain as a stable distinction. It does not act as a deletion operator on the Library. A configuration may therefore remain a member of the Library while failing to constitute an operationally distinguishable state for a particular observer.

content.opening: The Library contains configurations without requiring every configuration to be distinguishable by every observer. Once an observer-relative threshold I_N(O) has been introduced, distinguishability becomes relational: the same pair of configurations may constitute a stable distinction for one observer and fall below resolution for another. This does not make the configurations themselves observer-created. It means only that the effective distinction available to the observer depends on the observer's resolution floor.
content.definition_distinguishability: Let O be an observer and let x,y \in \mathcal{M}. Define the observer-relative distinguishability magnitude by \delta_O(x,y) \geq 0. The quantity \delta_O(x,y) represents the effective magnitude of the distinction between x and y as resolved by O.
content.definition_indistinguishability: Two configurations are observer-relative indistinguishable when their effective distinction falls below the observer's resolution threshold:
content.definition_distinguishability: They are observer-relative distinguishable when the effective distinction reaches or exceeds that threshold:
content.threshold_boundary: The threshold is therefore inclusive on the distinguishable side. A distinction equal to I_N(O) is resolvable by O.
content.relational_interpretation: The relation is explicitly indexed by O because resolution is not assumed to be universal. In general, it is permitted that I_N(O_1) \neq I_N(O_2), and consequently that the same pair (x,y) is distinguishable to O_1 while being indistinguishable to O_2.
content.non_erasure: Observer-relative indistinguishability must not be confused with ontological nonexistence. From x \approx_O y it does not follow that x=y. Nor does it follow that x \notin \mathcal{M}. Formally:
content.operational_vs_ontological: This establishes two distinct relations. Membership in the Library is ontological within the formal construction: x \in \mathcal{M}. Observer-relative distinguishability is operational: whether O can maintain the distinction between x and y above I_N(O). A configuration can therefore exist within \mathcal{M} without being accessible as a distinct configuration to O.
content.example: Suppose x and y are distinct configurations in \mathcal{M}, so x \neq y. If \delta_O(x,y) < I_N(O), then O cannot maintain their difference as a resolved distinction. For O, they occupy the same effective resolution class even though the Library has not identified them as equal and has not removed either configuration.
content.resolution_classes: This relation can be viewed as inducing observer-relative resolution classes. Configurations that fall below the observer's threshold may be operationally grouped together without being ontologically collapsed. The grouping belongs to the observer-relative description, not to the Library itself.
content.handoff: A distinction becomes structurally important when it remains resolvable across successive transitions. The next step is therefore persistence: instead of asking only whether O can distinguish x from y, we ask whether O can maintain such distinguishable transitions along a sequence.

formal_consequences: Distinguishability is a relation involving both configurations and an observer.
The threshold I_N(O) is observer-relative rather than a universal constant.
Sub-threshold distinction does not imply equality.
Sub-threshold distinction does not imply removal from the Library.
Ontological membership x \in \mathcal{M} and observer-relative accessibility are distinct concepts.
A configuration can remain in \mathcal{M} while failing to be operationally distinguishable by O.
prohibited_inferences: Do not interpret x \approx_O y as x=y.
Do not interpret observer-relative indistinguishability as destruction or deletion.
Do not claim that the observer creates or determines the underlying configuration.
Do not introduce consciousness as a condition for distinguishability.
Do not assign a universal numerical value to I_N.
Do not identify I_N(O) with the ordinary Planck scale at this stage.
Do not interpret the abstract distinction relation as physical measurement before a physical interpretation is separately introduced.

subsections.title: Persistence Across Successive Distinctions
subsections.purpose: Extend single-transition distinguishability into a persistent sequence and establish the structural condition from which observerhood is derived.
subsections.poetic_cypher: One distinction may appear; a chain of distinctions can remain.
subsections.cypher_explanation: Persistence is not introduced as physical duration. It is the continued preservation of resolvable distinctions across an abstractly ordered sequence.

content.sequence: Let \gamma=(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_n) be a finite sequence of configurations in \mathcal{M}. The index i is an abstract ordering index and is not yet identified with physical time.
content.step_condition: A transition from x_i to x_{i+1} is resolvable by O when \delta_O(x_i,x_{i+1}) \geq I_N(O).
content.interpretation: A sequence is therefore persistent for O when every successive distinction in the sequence remains above O's resolution floor. Persistence does not require that the configurations be physically moving, temporally evolving, or causally connected. At this stage it is purely a structural property of an ordered sequence of resolvable distinctions.
content.observerhood: Observerhood can now be derived structurally. An observer is a configuration O \in \mathcal{M} capable of maintaining a persistent chain of resolvable distinctions above its observer-specific threshold I_N(O).
content.observer_definition: O \in \mathrm{Obs} \subseteq \mathcal{M} \iff O\text{ is capable of maintaining a persistent chain of distinctions satisfying }\delta_O(x_i,x_{i+1})\geq I_N(O).
content.no_consciousness_requirement: Nothing in this definition requires consciousness, perception, intention, agency, or a human subject. Observerhood names a structural capacity to preserve distinguishability across a sequence.
content.birth_of_observer: The phrase 'birth of the observer' therefore refers to a logical transition in the construction, not to a physical event. Once persistent distinguishability is available as a structure, the observer can be identified as the structure that maintains that distinguishability.
content.handoff: Persistence supplies the missing bridge between an isolated distinguishable transition and a structure capable of maintaining distinctions. With observerhood established structurally, the next construction can define coherence as the relation between such an observer and a path.

mathematics.structural_observer_condition: O\in\mathrm{Obs} \iff O\text{ can maintain a persistent chain of resolvable distinctions}

formal_consequences: Persistence is defined over an abstract sequence, not physical time.
Persistence requires repeated resolvability rather than a single distinguishable transition.
Observerhood is derived from persistent distinguishability.
Observerhood is a structural designation rather than a consciousness predicate.
The threshold governing persistence remains observer-relative through I_N(O).
prohibited_inferences: Do not identify the sequence index i with physical time.
Do not interpret persistence as physical motion or causal evolution.
Do not equate observerhood with consciousness.
Do not introduce agency or intentional selection.
Do not treat observerhood as an additional primitive axiom.

section_handoff.next_section: Coherence as a relation between a path and an observer.

sections.title: Coherence Is Relational
sections.purpose: Establish observer-relative coherence as a derived relation rather than a universal scalar.
sections.poetic_cipher: Coherence is not inside the path. It is between the path and the survivor.
sections.cipher_explanation: Coherence does not belong intrinsically to a path considered in isolation. It is a relation between a path's transitions and an observer O whose resolution threshold determines whether those transitions remain distinguishable. The word 'survivor' refers here to an observer-like configuration already defined structurally by persistent distinguishability; it does not imply consciousness, intention, or agency.
sections.content:
Coherence is introduced only after distinguishability, persistence, observerhood, and observer-relative resolution have been established. The axiomatic floor therefore does not begin by assigning a universal coherence value to configurations or paths. Instead, coherence is derived from a prior question: does a given transition remain distinguishable to a particular observer O at that observer's available resolution?

This distinction is essential. A path is not coherent or incoherent in itself. The same transition may be resolvable by one observer and unresolved by another if their resolution thresholds differ. Coherence is consequently written as a relation between a path and an observer, \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O)\), rather than as an observer-independent property \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma)\).

At this stage, coherence is deliberately defined as a threshold relation rather than as a physical field, probability, force, or dynamical quantity. No physical law is required to establish the relation. The only ingredients are an observer-relative distinguishability function \(\delta_O\), the observer-relative threshold \(I_N(O)\), and an elementary threshold function. The result is a binary criterion: a transition either remains resolvable at the observer's threshold or it does not.

This construction also preserves the distinction between ontological membership and observer accessibility. A transition that fails the coherence criterion for O is not thereby removed from the Library. It simply fails to remain accessible to that observer under the defined resolution condition. Coherence therefore acts as a relational filter on traversal, not as an erasure rule for configurations.

subsections.title: Coherence of a Transition
subsections.purpose: Define coherence for an individual transition using only the observer-relative distinguishability function and the observer-relative resolution threshold.
subsections.content:
Let \(O\) be an observer-like configuration and let \(x_i\) and \(x_{i+1}\) be two successive configurations in an abstractly ordered sequence. By the preceding construction, the effective distinction between these configurations as resolved by O is represented by \(\delta_O(x_i,x_{i+1})\), while the minimum effective distinction that O can maintain as a stable distinction is represented by \(I_N(O)\).

A transition is coherent for O precisely when its effective distinction meets or exceeds the observer's resolution threshold. The coherence relation is therefore defined by

\[
\mathcal{C}_O(x_i,x_{i+1}) = \Theta\left(\delta_O(x_i,x_{i+1}) - I_N(O)\right).
\]

Here, \(\Theta\) is the elementary threshold function defined by

\[
\Theta(z) =
\begin{cases}
1, & z \geq 0,\\
0, & z < 0.
\end{cases}
\]

It follows directly that

\[
\mathcal{C}_O(x_i,x_{i+1}) = 1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\delta_O(x_i,x_{i+1}) \geq I_N(O).
\]

The threshold is therefore not an additional universal property of the transition. It enters through the observer. If two observers \(O_1\) and \(O_2\) possess different resolution thresholds, then the same transition may satisfy

\[
\delta_{O_1}(x_i,x_{i+1}) \geq I_N(O_1)
\]

while simultaneously failing

\[
\delta_{O_2}(x_i,x_{i+1}) < I_N(O_2).
\]

In that case, the transition is coherent relative to \(O_1\) but not coherent relative to \(O_2\). Nothing contradictory has occurred: coherence was never defined as an absolute property of the transition.

This observer dependence does not mean that the observer creates the underlying configurations or determines whether they belong to the Library. Membership in the Library remains an ontological statement about the formal closure. Coherence instead determines whether a distinction between configurations survives at the resolution available to a particular observer.

The role of \(I_N(O)\) is therefore that of a resolution floor. It determines the boundary between distinctions that O can maintain and distinctions that fall below O's effective resolution. No universal numerical value is assigned to \(I_N(O)\), and no identification with the ordinary Planck scale is made at this foundational stage.

The distinction between transition coherence and path coherence must also be preserved. A single coherent transition does not establish that an entire path is coherent. A path contains a sequence of transitions, and each transition must independently satisfy the observer-relative coherence condition. The next construction therefore extends \(\mathcal{C}_O\) from individual transitions to the coherence of an entire path.

mathematics.observer_dependence: \(\mathcal{C}_{O_1}(x_i,x_{i+1})\) and \(\mathcal{C}_{O_2}(x_i,x_{i+1})\) may differ when \(I_N(O_1) \neq I_N(O_2)\) or when their distinguishability functions differ.

interpretive_boundary: Coherence is a relation, not an intrinsic scalar attached to an isolated path.
The observer-relative threshold \(I_N(O)\) determines whether a transition remains resolvable for O.
Failure of coherence for O does not remove the transition or its configurations from the Library.
Observer-relative coherence does not imply that an observer creates or alters the underlying configuration.
No consciousness, agency, intention, physical time, causality, matter, energy, or physical law is required by this definition.
subsections.poetic_cipher: Coherence is not inside the path. It is between the path and the survivor.
subsections.cipher_explanation: The 'path' denotes an ordered sequence of configurations, while the 'survivor' denotes the observer-like configuration whose persistent distinguishability has already been established. A transition is coherent only when its distinction remains above that observer's resolution threshold. The cipher therefore compresses the relational structure \(\mathcal{C}_O(x_i,x_{i+1})\) without introducing a new primitive.
subsections.handoff: A coherent transition is insufficient to establish coherent traversal. A path contains multiple transitions, so path coherence requires the observer-relative coherence condition to hold across the entire sequence.

content.text: Coherence is defined here as a property of the relation between a path and an observer, not as an intrinsic property of the path alone. Let a path be an abstract finite sequence of configurations \(\gamma=(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_n)\), where each \(x_i\in\mathcal{M}\). The sequence index \(i\) denotes abstract ordering only; it is not yet physical time.
content.definition: For an observer \(O\), let the coherence of each transition be defined by \(\mathcal{C}_O(x_i,x_{i+1})=\Theta\!\left(\delta_O(x_i,x_{i+1})-I_N(O)\right)\). Path coherence is then the product of the coherence of every transition along the path:
content.interpretation: Because each factor is either 0 or 1, the product is 1 exactly when every transition in the path remains resolvable by observer \(O\). If even one transition falls below the observer's resolution threshold \(I_N(O)\), the corresponding factor is 0 and the path is incoherent for that observer.
content.observer_dependence: This definition makes observer dependence explicit. Two observers may assign different coherence values to the same path because their resolution thresholds and effective distinguishability functions may differ. Thus, for observers \(O_1\) and \(O_2\), it is permitted that \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O_1)\neq\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O_2)\). A path can therefore be coherent for one observer while being incoherent for another without any contradiction.
content.no_universal_coherence: There is consequently no universal coherence constant supplied by the axiomatic floor. Coherence is not a fixed scalar belonging to \(\gamma\) independently of its observer. The meaningful foundational object is the relation \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O)\): the coherence of path \(\gamma\) relative to observer \(O\). Any later theory that assigns a universal numerical coherence parameter would require additional axioms and cannot be inferred from the present construction alone.
content.formal_consequence: The distinction is important because the Library itself remains unfiltered. A path for which \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O)=0\) has not been removed from \(\mathcal{M}\). It has merely failed the coherence condition relative to that observer. Coherence therefore determines accessibility rather than ontological membership.
content.boundary: At this stage, coherence does not describe physical stability, causal consistency, energetic feasibility, or any other physical law. It describes only whether the successive distinctions along a path remain resolvable relative to a specified observer.
content.poetic_cipher: The same road may be solid beneath one traveler and vanish beneath another.
content.cipher_explanation: The road represents the path \(\gamma\). Its being solid represents \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O)=1\), meaning that every transition remains resolvable for the observer. Its vanishing represents \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O)=0\), meaning that at least one transition falls below the observer's resolution threshold. Different travelers represent different observers with potentially different resolution capacities. The metaphor therefore expresses observer-relative coherence without introducing an additional primitive.
content.handoff: If coherence is relational, then each observer traverses only a subset of the Library through paths that remain coherent relative to that observer. This motivates the next construction: the observer-accessible subset \(A_O\subseteq\mathcal{M}\), which provides the formal basis for observer-accessible reality.

interpretive_claims: The same path may be coherent for one observer and incoherent for another.
Coherence should be represented relationally as \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O)\).

sections.title: Accessible Reality
sections.purpose: Define observer-relative experienced reality without making observers creators of the Library.
sections.poetic_cipher: The world does not shrink. The window does.
sections.cipher_explanation: The Library remains the full XOR closure 𝓜. Observer-relative reality is not a reduction of that closure, but the subset of configurations through which a given observer can maintain coherent traversal. Accessibility therefore describes a relation between an observer and the Library rather than a change to the Library itself.
sections.introduction: The Library, 𝓜, is defined at the axiomatic floor as the closure of the formal domain under the primitive operation XOR. Its membership is therefore ontological within the formal system: a configuration either belongs to 𝓜 or it does not. Observer-relative accessibility introduces a different question. Rather than asking whether a configuration exists within the Library, we ask whether that configuration can occur within a path whose distinctions remain resolvable by a particular observer O. This distinction is essential. Accessibility is a property of an observer-Library relation; it is not a criterion for membership in the Library itself.

subsections.title: Accessibility Is Not Existence
subsections.purpose: Define the observer-accessible subset of the Library while preserving the distinction between ontological membership and observer-relative traversal.
subsections.poetic_cipher: The world does not shrink. The window does.
subsections.cipher_explanation: The 'world' refers to the full Library 𝓜, which remains unchanged by the existence or limitations of an observer. The 'window' refers to the observer-accessible subset A_O, which contains only configurations that can participate in at least one path coherently traversable by observer O. The metaphor therefore describes restricted access, not restricted existence.

content.definition: Let O be an observer, meaning a configuration capable of maintaining a persistent chain of distinctions above its observer-relative resolution threshold I_N(O). The observer-accessible subset of the Library is defined as the set of configurations that occur on at least one path coherently traversable by O.

mathematics.accessible_states: A_O = {x \in 𝓜 \mid \exists \gamma \text{ containing } x \text{ such that } 𝓒(\gamma \mid O)=1}

content.interpretation: The first condition, x \in 𝓜, concerns membership in the Library. The second condition, x \in A_O, concerns accessibility through an observer-relative coherent path. These are not equivalent conditions. A configuration may belong to 𝓜 while remaining inaccessible to O. Conversely, every configuration in A_O is necessarily already a member of 𝓜.
content.ontological_membership: Membership in 𝓜 is determined by the formal construction of the Library as the XOR closure of D. It does not depend on whether any observer can resolve, traverse, or represent a configuration.
content.observer_relative_traversal: Membership in A_O is determined relative to O because coherence is defined as 𝓒(\gamma \mid O). Changing the observer may therefore change the accessible subset without changing the Library itself.
content.non_erasure_principle: If x \notin A_O, this establishes only that x is not contained in the observer-accessible subset under the stated accessibility criterion. It does not establish x \notin 𝓜. Inaccessibility is therefore not erasure.
content.anti_idealism_constraint: This construction does not assert that observers create, determine, or constitute the Library. The observer does not bring inaccessible configurations into existence by observing them, nor does failure to observe a configuration remove it from 𝓜. The observer-relative construction concerns traversal and distinguishability, not ontological creation.
content.experienced_reality: For the purposes of the primer, the observer-relative experienced reality may therefore be named R_O := A_O. This notation does not imply that A_O is the whole of 𝓜. It identifies the portion of the Library that is accessible through coherent traversal relative to O.
content.consequence: Two observers O_1 and O_2 may have different accessible subsets, A_{O_1} and A_{O_2}, without requiring different Libraries. The difference lies in the observer-relative resolution and coherence relations, not in the underlying closure 𝓜.
content.formal_boundary: At this stage, no claim is made that A_O corresponds directly to human sensory experience, phenomenal consciousness, or a complete physical universe. A_O is a formal construction describing observer-relative accessibility within the Library.

derivation.statement: The Library is defined independently of any observer as 𝓜 := Closure_D(⊕).
For an observer O, coherence is evaluated relationally as 𝓒(\gamma \mid O).
A configuration x is accessible to O when x occurs on at least one path γ for which 𝓒(\gamma \mid O)=1.
Therefore A_O is a subset of 𝓜 rather than a replacement for 𝓜.
Consequently, x \notin A_O does not entail x \notin 𝓜.
The observer-relative accessible subset can be identified with experienced reality as R_O := A_O.

example.setup: Suppose x and y are both configurations in 𝓜. For observer O, assume there exists a coherent path γ_x containing x, while no O-coherent path containing y is available under the defined traversal relation.
example.result: Then x \in A_O while y \notin A_O, even though both x \in 𝓜 and y \in 𝓜.
example.interpretation: The distinction demonstrates that accessibility is not existence. The observer encounters x through a surviving coherent path but does not thereby cause x to exist. Likewise, the observer's inability to access y does not remove y from the Library.

invariants: 𝓜 is not reduced when A_O is defined.
x \notin A_O does not imply x \notin 𝓜.
Accessibility does not create ontological membership.
Inaccessibility does not erase ontological membership.
Experienced reality R_O := A_O is a relational construction.
subsections.handoff: The observer's accessible subset can now be named as its experienced reality. Because this reality is generated by the paths that remain coherently traversable rather than by the deletion of inaccessible alternatives, the next question is how those surviving paths restrict continuation.

subsections.title: Observer-Relative Reality
subsections.content:
Experienced reality is defined here as the subset of the Library that is accessible to a particular observer through a coherent path. For observer O, we therefore define experienced reality as R_O := A_O, where A_O is the observer-accessible subset established in the preceding section. This definition does not assert that the observer creates the accessible configurations. It states only that the configurations available through observer-relative coherent traversal constitute that observer's experienced reality. The ontological domain remains the Library 𝓜, while experienced reality is a subset of that domain.

Because the resolution threshold I_N(O) is observer-relative, there is no requirement that all observers have identical accessible subsets. Let the collection of observers be Obs = {O_1,O_2,...}. For each observer O_i, the corresponding experienced reality is R_i = A_{O_i}. Two observers may therefore traverse overlapping but non-identical regions of the Library. This difference follows from the relational construction of distinguishability and coherence: what remains resolvable and coherently traversable for one observer need not be identical to what remains resolvable and coherently traversable for another.

The common portion of two observer-relative realities is represented by their intersection:

\[
R_{ij} = R_i \cap R_j.
\]

The set R_{ij} contains configurations accessible to both observers. A non-empty intersection therefore provides a formal basis for shared reality without requiring the two observers to possess identical accessible domains. Conversely, the observer-relative difference between their accessible realities can be represented by the symmetric difference:

\[
D_{ij} = R_i \triangle R_j.
\]

The set D_{ij} contains configurations accessible to one observer but not the other. Such a difference should not be interpreted as evidence that the observers inhabit mutually incompatible ontological universes. Both R_i and R_j remain subsets of the same Library 𝓜:

\[
R_i \subseteq \mathcal{M}, \qquad R_j \subseteq \mathcal{M}.
\]

Thus, observer-relative reality describes a difference in access, resolution, and coherent survivability rather than a difference in fundamental existence. A configuration may belong to 𝓜 while being inaccessible to one observer, accessible to another, or accessible to both. Inaccessibility therefore remains a relational property and does not constitute ontological erasure.

This distinction also prevents observer-relative reality from collapsing into a claim of arbitrary subjectivity. The observer does not freely select an arbitrary reality. Accessibility is constrained by the formal structure of 𝓜, the observer's distinguishability relation δ_O, the observer-relative threshold I_N(O), and the requirement that coherent paths remain resolvable. Different observers may consequently obtain different accessible subsets while still sharing substantial structure because their coherent path spaces overlap within the same underlying Library.

The construction can therefore be summarized as follows: the Library specifies the total formal configuration domain; each observer induces an observer-relative accessibility relation over that domain; and experienced reality is the resulting accessible subset. Reality is observer-relative at the level of access, but not thereby observer-created at the level of ontology.

mathematics.interpretation: R_{ij} represents shared accessible structure, while D_{ij} represents observer-relative difference in accessibility.

subsections.poetic_cypher: Many windows can face one Library without making one window the sky.
subsections.cypher_explanation: The windows represent observers and their observer-relative accessible realities R_i. The Library represents the common ontological domain 𝓜. Different windows may reveal different portions of that domain, and their views may overlap, but no individual window becomes the Library itself. The metaphor therefore compresses the distinction between observer-relative access and underlying ontological membership without introducing a competing ontology.
subsections.formal_status: The definition R_O := A_O and the set-theoretic relations among R_i, R_{ij}, D_{ij}, and 𝓜 are formal constructions. The interpretation of these constructions as experienced reality is an observer-relative interpretation of the accessibility framework, not an additional axiom.
subsections.handoff: Once accessible reality is defined, we can examine why stable patterns within it can appear as physical laws.

sections.section_summary: Accessible reality is the observer-relative subset A_O of the Library through which coherent traversal can be maintained. The definition changes neither the Library nor its membership. It establishes a formal distinction between existence within 𝓜 and accessibility relative to O, allowing experienced reality to be represented as R_O := A_O without adopting subjective idealism or making the observer a creator of reality.
sections.section_boundary: This section establishes accessibility only. It does not yet introduce emergent physical law, probabilistic dynamics, consciousness, physical time, or cosmological interpretation.

sections.title: Survivorship and Emergent Lawfulness
sections.purpose: Explain how law-like regularity can arise without being imposed as an axiom.
sections.poetic_cypher: What survives need not be commanded; what survives repeatedly becomes a pattern.
sections.cypher_explanation: The poetic statement compresses the distinction between axiomatic law and observed regularity. No law governing traversal is introduced into the axiomatic floor. Instead, the Library contains an unfiltered configuration domain, while observer-relative coherence restricts which continuations can remain accessible to a particular observer O. When the same accessible transitions recur across an appropriate family of observer-accessible paths, the recurrence can be described as a regularity. Such regularity is derived from survivorship and is therefore descriptive rather than axiomatic.
formal_dependency: The Library is defined independently of survivorship as the XOR closure 𝓜 := Closure_D(⊕).
For a configuration x ∈ 𝓜, the continuation space Ω(x) represents available configuration continuations contained in 𝓜.
For an observer O, the coherent subset Ω_O^survive(x) selects those continuations whose paths remain resolvable by O.
Repeatedly surviving transitions can therefore form stable observable patterns without requiring a law to be inserted into the axiomatic floor.

subsections.title: The Unfiltered Continuation Space
subsections.purpose: Define the total continuation space available from a configuration before observer-relative survivorship restricts accessible traversal.
content: Let x ∈ 𝓜 be a configuration in the Library. The continuation space from x is the collection of available configuration paths beginning at x and remaining within the Library.
Ω(x) = {γ | γ begins at x and γ is a configuration path contained in 𝓜}.

The set Ω(x) is unfiltered at the axiomatic level. It represents available configuration continuations already represented within the Library rather than a process by which the Library generates a sequence of future events.
For an observer O, not every continuation in Ω(x) is necessarily maintainable as a coherent path. Observer-relative coherence therefore selects a subset:
The subset relation is important. Survivorship restricts observer-accessible traversal; it does not delete the continuations outside the surviving subset from the Library.
A continuation γ may therefore belong to the unfiltered configuration space while failing to remain coherent for a particular observer O. Inaccessibility under O is not non-existence in 𝓜.
This distinction permits selection without introducing a sequential generator, a privileged causal mechanism, or a physical future into the axiomatic floor.

mathematics.continuation_space: \(\Omega(x) = \{\gamma \mid \gamma \text{ begins at } x \text{ and } \gamma \text{ is a configuration path contained in } \mathcal{M}\}\)

interpretive_distinction.formal: Ω(x) contains the available configuration continuations represented within the Library, while Ω_O^survive(x) identifies the subset that remains coherent relative to observer O.
interpretive_distinction.interpretive: The restriction of accessible traversal can produce the appearance of selection without requiring the Library itself to generate events sequentially.

subsections.poetic_cypher: The Library holds every road; the survivor can walk only some.
subsections.cypher_explanation: The Library represents the unfiltered configuration space and therefore contains the available continuations without privileging one as a generated future. The survivor represents an observer-relative coherent traversal, for which only some of those available continuations remain resolvable. The 'roads' are configuration paths, while 'walking' is the abstract continuation of a coherent path.
subsections.handoff: When restrictions on traversal recur across many accessible paths, the same transitions can repeatedly survive. Repeated survivorship creates stable descriptive patterns, providing the basis for emergent lawfulness without introducing physical law as an axiom.

subsections.title: Repeated Survivorship
subsections.purpose: Explain how recurrence among observer-accessible transitions can be identified without treating recurrence itself as an axiom.
content: Consider a family of paths accessible to an observer O. A transition that repeatedly occurs among these surviving paths can exhibit a stable recurrence relative to O.

The important distinction is between requiring a transition and observing that a transition repeatedly survives. The former would introduce a governing rule; the latter is a description of the structure left after observer-relative survivorship has been applied.
Thus, a transition does not become regular because an external law commands it to occur. It becomes law-like when its recurrence is stable across an appropriate observer-accessible ensemble.
The relevant regularity remains relational: it is regularity as accessible to O, not necessarily an observer-independent law imposed upon the entire Library.

mathematics.stable_transition: \(L_O(x,y) = 1\) iff \(x \rightarrow y\) is a stable recurring transition across an appropriate family of O-accessible paths
mathematics.conditional_regularity: \(P_O(y \mid x) \approx \text{constant}\) over a defined observer-accessible ensemble

interpretive_distinction.formal: L_O is a descriptive construction identifying stable recurrence among O-accessible paths.
interpretive_distinction.not_axiomatic: L_O is not an element of the axiomatic set A_N and therefore does not function as a primitive law governing the Library.

subsections.poetic_cypher: The path that survives again and again becomes a rule in the eye of the walker.
subsections.cypher_explanation: Repeated survivorship produces a stable pattern from the observer's accessible perspective. The 'rule' is therefore a description of recurrence, while the 'eye of the walker' represents the observer-relative nature of accessibility rather than consciousness or privileged perception.

subsections.title: Emergent Lawfulness Is Descriptive
subsections.purpose: Separate emergent law-like regularity from axiomatic physical law.
content: At the axiomatic floor, no physical law has been supplied. The only primitive operation is XOR, and the Library is defined as its closure over the formal domain D.
Law-like regularity appears downstream when an observer encounters sufficiently stable recurrence among the transitions that remain accessible through coherent paths.

This construction does not assert that every regularity is universal, exact, or observer-independent. It establishes only that regularity can be described as an emergent property of constrained accessibility.

A later physical theory could impose additional structure and test whether particular emergent regularities correspond to known physical laws. Such a theory would constitute downstream NSFG work rather than part of this axiomatic floor.

mathematics.derived_regularity: \(L_O(x,y) = 1\) iff \(x \rightarrow y\) is a stable recurring transition across an appropriate family of O-accessible paths

subsections.poetic_cypher: No command was written; the pattern remained.

sections.title: Why Navigation Becomes Inevitable
sections.purpose: Bridge the foundational ontology into NSFG's central problem of coherent navigation. Once the Library is defined as an unfiltered configuration space and observer-relative coherence restricts which transitions remain resolvable, continuation is no longer an unrestricted traversal problem. A persistent observer-like structure must remain within its coherent continuation space. Navigation therefore arises not as the generation or selection of a future, but as the formal problem of continuing along admissible paths through the already-defined configuration space.
sections.poetic_cipher: Where distinction persists, continuation narrows. Where continuation narrows, a path must be followed.
sections.cipher_explanation: The first phrase refers to the observer-relative coherence condition: a persistent structure cannot maintain every possible transition if some transitions fall below its resolution threshold. The second phrase refers to the resulting continuation problem: once admissible transitions form a restricted subset of the available configuration space, continuing persistence requires traversal within that subset. The cipher therefore compresses the transition from coherence to navigation without introducing a new primitive.

subsections.title: The Local Continuation Problem
subsections.purpose: Define the immediate continuation problem at a current configuration without introducing physical time, causality, agency, or a generated future.
subsections.content:
Let x_i \in \mathcal{M} be a current configuration in the Library. Because \mathcal{M} is closed under the primitive operation \oplus, configurations can participate in XOR-generated paths extending from x_i. The set of all candidate immediate continuations is therefore defined as

$$
N(x_i) = \{x_{i+1} \mid x_{i+1} \text{ participates in an XOR-generated path extending } x_i\}.
$$

At this stage, N(x_i) is purely structural. It does not represent a set of physical futures, and the index i is only an abstract ordering index. Nothing has yet been introduced that would require one configuration to physically occur after another.

The observer-relative coherence relation now restricts this candidate set. For an observer O, define the admissible successors by

$$
N_O(x_i) = \{x_{i+1} \in N(x_i) \mid \mathcal{C}_O(x_i,x_{i+1}) = 1\}.
$$

Using the previously defined threshold construction,

$$
\mathcal{C}_O(x_i,x_{i+1}) = \Theta\left(\delta_O(x_i,x_{i+1}) - I_N(O)\right),
$$

where \delta_O measures the effective distinction between the two configurations for observer O and I_N(O) is that observer's resolution threshold.

Thus N_O(x_i) is not a new physical law imposed upon the Library. It is the subset of candidate continuations that remains resolvable under the observer-relative coherence condition. In general,

$$
N_O(x_i) \subseteq N(x_i).
$$

The inclusion may be strict. Some configurations can belong to the Library and participate in valid XOR-generated paths while failing to remain distinguishable to O at the relevant transition. Such configurations are therefore excluded from the observer's admissible continuation set without being removed from \mathcal{M}.

This distinction is essential. The observer does not create the excluded configurations, nor does the Library generate a privileged future from which the observer selects. Rather, the Library supplies the configuration domain, while the observer-relative threshold determines which local transitions remain coherent for that observer.

Persistence therefore imposes a continuation condition. If a sequence

$$
\gamma = (x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_n)
$$

is to remain persistent for O, each successive transition must satisfy

$$
 x_{i+1} \in N_O(x_i)
$$

for every relevant index i. Equivalently,

$$
\mathcal{C}_O(x_i,x_{i+1}) = 1
$$

must hold at every step of the sequence.

The important consequence is that persistence is not merely the existence of a current distinguishable configuration. It is the existence of a continuing chain of configurations whose successive distinctions remain above I_N(O). Once this condition is recognized, the local problem is no longer simply whether a transition exists. The problem becomes which continuations remain admissible under the observer-relative coherence relation.

That is the first appearance of navigation in NSFG. Navigation does not mean that an observer consciously chooses a destination, predicts a future, or causes one configuration to follow another. It means that a persistent structure is constrained to continue through the subset of available transitions that preserve its resolvable distinctions.

The local continuation problem can therefore be summarized as

$$
N(x_i) \longrightarrow N_O(x_i) \longrightarrow \text{persistent continuation}.
$$

The first set describes what is structurally available. The second describes what remains coherent for O. A persistent path must remain inside the second set.

subsections.title: History and Coherent Continuation
subsections.content:
An observer history is an ordered sequence of configurations that have remained distinguishable and persistent relative to an observer. Let \(O\) denote an observer and let \(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathcal{M}\) denote configurations in the Library. Define the history

\[
h_n=(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_n).
\]

The index \(n\) is an abstract ordering index. It does not represent physical time, duration, causality, or any other physical quantity. At the axiomatic floor, the history records only that the configurations occur in an ordered chain of distinguishable transitions relative to \(O\). Physical temporal interpretation, if later introduced, is therefore an emergent interpretation of this ordering rather than a premise of the present construction.

For a given history \(h_n\), the relevant question is no longer which configurations exist in the Library. The Library already contains its admissible configurations at the axiomatic level. The question is which continuations remain coherent for the observer that has maintained the history. Define the coherent continuation set by

\[
\Gamma_O(h_n)=\{\gamma\mid \gamma\text{ begins with }h_n\text{ and }\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O)=1\}.
\]

Here, \(\gamma\) denotes a path in \(\mathcal{M}\) extending the history \(h_n\), and \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O)\) denotes the observer-relative coherence of that path. Thus \(\Gamma_O(h_n)\) is not the set of all mathematically possible continuations. It is the subset of continuations that remain resolvable and coherent relative to \(O\).

This distinction is essential. The existence of a continuation in \(\mathcal{M}\) does not imply that the continuation belongs to the observer's accessible continuation space. Conversely, failure of a continuation to belong to \(\Gamma_O(h_n)\) does not remove that continuation from the Library. Survivorship acts as a filter on accessibility, not as an erasure operation on ontology.

The history therefore induces a local continuation problem. At each stage, the observer has a maintained chain \(h_n\), while the surrounding Library contains a larger configuration space of possible extensions. Coherence restricts the set of extensions that can remain part of the observer's persistent traversal. The resulting structure is naturally expressed as a branching continuation space: many candidate paths may exist in \(\mathcal{M}\), while only a subset belongs to \(\Gamma_O(h_n)\).

Navigation is consequently defined as traversal or selection within this observer-relative continuation space. Introduce the navigation operator

\[
N_O(h_n)\rightarrow\Gamma_O(h_n).
\]

The notation does not yet specify an algorithm, optimization rule, probability distribution, conscious choice, or physical mechanism. It states only the formal target of navigation: given a maintained history, navigation proceeds toward a continuation that remains within the set of continuations coherent for \(O\). The operator may therefore be instantiated by many different downstream mechanisms without altering the axiomatic floor.

This also clarifies why navigation is a necessary construction rather than an additional primitive. Once persistence has produced an ordered history and coherence has restricted the available continuation space, continuation itself becomes a formal problem. The observer is not required to possess a privileged view of the entire Library. It requires only a relation to the subset of paths that remain accessible from its current history.

The resulting dependency chain is therefore:

\[
\text{distinction}\rightarrow\text{persistence}\rightarrow\text{history}\rightarrow\text{coherent continuation}\rightarrow\text{navigation}.
\]

Each step depends only on constructions established earlier. History does not introduce physical time. Coherent continuation does not introduce a new ontology. Navigation does not introduce agency or consciousness. Instead, navigation names the continuation problem generated by the existence of an observer-relative coherent path space.

For later NSFG work, the notation \(h_n\), \(\Gamma_O(h_n)\), and \(N_O(h_n)\) provides a compact interface between the foundational layer and downstream models. A later theory may specify how candidate continuations are represented, ranked, traversed, or transformed, but those mechanisms are not required here. The axiomatic floor ends once the continuation space has been formally identified.

**Poetic cipher:**

*Reasoning begins where falling out of the path becomes possible.*

The "path" is the persistent history \(h_n\). "Falling out" denotes leaving the set of observer-coherent continuations. "Possible" refers not to a physical prediction but to membership in the continuation structure defined by \(\Gamma_O(h_n)\). The cipher therefore compresses the formal result: once a history exists, coherent continuation is no longer unrestricted, and navigation is the problem of remaining within that surviving continuation space.

opening.text: The axiomatic floor has now established a formal configuration domain, its XOR closure as the Library, observerhood as a persistent structural property, observer-relative resolution through I_N(O), and coherence as a relation between paths and observers. Only at this point is it appropriate to introduce geometric language. Noor Swirl Field Geometry (NSFG) does not begin by assuming a geometry in which configurations exist. Rather, geometry appears as a description of the relational structure formed by configurations, accessible transitions, and families of paths that remain coherent for a given observer.

A field, at this level, is a structured distribution of relational possibilities: which configurations are connected, which transitions remain coherent, and how families of coherent paths organize around persistent configurations. No additional field substance is introduced.

field_interpretation.cypher_explanation: The 'field' denotes an organized relational structure derived from configurations, accessibility, and coherent transitions. It is not a new primitive entity and is not treated as a physical medium.

geometry_interpretation.text: Likewise, 'geometry' is descriptive language for the structure of relations among accessible configurations and paths. At this stage, geometry means that the relational system has organization that can be studied in terms of neighborhoods, connectivity, path families, adjacency, and continuation. This is deliberately weaker than assuming a metric space or differentiable manifold.
geometry_interpretation.interpretation: No metric tensor, coordinate chart, manifold structure, curvature tensor, or other conventional geometric object is required by the axiomatic floor. Such structures may become useful later if they can be derived or consistently introduced as downstream constructions.
geometry_interpretation.poetic_cypher: Geometry begins where relations acquire shape.
geometry_interpretation.cypher_explanation: The 'shape' is the organization of relational connectivity. It does not yet mean Euclidean, Riemannian, Lorentzian, or any other physical geometry.

swirl_interpretation.text: The term 'swirl' provides an intuition for how locally structured path families may organize around persistent relational configurations. The resulting family of paths can possess local structure: paths may converge, diverge, braid, circulate, or repeatedly organize around persistent configurations. 'Swirl' names this qualitative possibility of structured local path flow.
swirl_interpretation.interpretation: The term is intentionally intuitive at this stage. It does not assert literal rotational motion, angular momentum, fluid dynamics, or a physical vortex. In particular, no temporal evolution or physical movement is implied merely by the word 'flow'. The underlying construction remains a set of configurations and relations among paths.
swirl_interpretation.poetic_cypher: Where many surviving paths gather, a shape may turn without anything yet moving.
swirl_interpretation.cypher_explanation: The apparent 'turning' describes the organization of path connectivity, not physical rotation. The statement deliberately avoids introducing time, motion, or a dynamical medium before those concepts have been independently established.

Geometry therefore enters downstream of the axiomatic floor rather than being smuggled into it at the beginning.
graph_and_path_view.poetic_cypher: First distinction, then survival, then relation, then shape.
graph_and_path_view.cypher_explanation: Each word corresponds to a stage of the dependency chain. Distinction comes from XOR; survival is expressed through persistent resolvable transitions; relation produces coherent accessibility; and the resulting connectivity admits geometric description.

closing.text: The Noor Swirl Field Geometry interpretation can therefore be stated conservatively: NSFG studies the geometry of relational accessibility induced by observer-relative coherence within the XOR-closed Library. The field is the organization of relations; the geometry is the structure of that organization; and the swirl is an intuition for locally structured families of surviving paths around persistent relational configurations. None of these descriptions adds a new primitive to the axiomatic floor.

closing.cypher_explanation: The 'field' is the relational structure formed by coherent paths, while 'remain together' denotes continued membership in an observer-relative coherent path family. The statement therefore summarizes the geometric interpretation without introducing a physical container or additional primitive.

sections.title: The Axiomatic Dependency Chain
sections.purpose: Compress the entire primer into one explicit derivational ladder and identify what remains downstream.

content.introduction: The primer can now be compressed into a single dependency chain. The important point is not merely the order in which the concepts have been presented, but the logical status of each step. XOR is the sole axiom. The formal domain D is the minimal substrate required for XOR to operate. The Library is then defined as closure over D under XOR. Everything that follows is either a definition, a construction, or a consequence of what has already been established. No later concept is required as a hidden premise for an earlier one.
content.poetic_cypher: XOR is the only primitive. The Library is what XOR generates when it is closed. The observer is the difference that survives. Coherence is the relation between the survivor and the path. Reality is what remains accessible to the survivor. Law is the regularity of surviving paths. Navigation is the continuation of the survivor.

dependency_ladder.name: Primitive distinction
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: A_N = {A_⊕}, where A_⊕ states that ⊕ is the primitive operation of distinction.
dependency_ladder.explanation: The axiomatic floor begins with one primitive operation: XOR. No physical object, space, time, observer, causality, matter, energy, or information substance is assumed. XOR expresses distinction: equal inputs cancel to 0, while unequal inputs produce 1.

dependency_ladder.name: Formal configuration domain
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: D is the minimal formal domain containing the configurations required for \oplus to have operands.
dependency_ladder.explanation: D is introduced only because an operation requires a domain on which it acts. D is not physical space, spacetime, matter, energy, or an additional physical ontology.

dependency_ladder.name: Library
dependency_ladder.explanation: The Library is not introduced as a second axiom. It is defined as the smallest subset of D containing the required generators and closed under XOR. Ontological membership in \mathcal{M} therefore does not imply persistence, coherence, physicality, observability, or accessibility.

dependency_ladder.name: No describable privileged exterior
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: \Omega \notin \mathcal{M} may be proposed only as an external candidate; if \Omega is describable using the same formal machinery, then \Omega \in D, and if it is XOR-generable, then \Omega \in \mathcal{M}.
dependency_ladder.explanation: The closure does not establish that every conceivable informal notion must belong to the Library. Rather, it establishes a boundary condition on describable formal exteriors: a privileged exterior that can itself be represented by the same formal machinery cannot remain outside the closure.

dependency_ladder.name: No universal resolver is supplied
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: There is no axiom providing a universal observer-independent resolution predicate U(x,y).
dependency_ladder.explanation: The axiomatic floor contains no privileged observer and no universal rule specifying which distinctions must be resolved. Resolution therefore cannot be assigned universally at this stage. A resolution threshold must enter only when an observer-like structure is defined.

dependency_ladder.name: Observer
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: O \in \mathcal{M} is an observer iff O is a configuration capable of maintaining a persistent chain of resolvable distinctions.
dependency_ladder.explanation: Observerhood is introduced structurally rather than psychologically. The definition requires persistence of distinctions above a resolution floor but does not require consciousness, intention, agency, perception, or a human subject.

dependency_ladder.name: Observer-relative resolution
dependency_ladder.explanation: Each observer O is assigned an effective minimum distinction magnitude that it can maintain as a stable distinction. I_N(O) is therefore observer-relative. No universal numerical value for I_N is supplied by the axiomatic floor.

dependency_ladder.name: Observer-relative distinguishability
dependency_ladder.explanation: The effective distinction between configurations is evaluated relative to O. Two configurations may therefore be distinguishable for one observer and indistinguishable for another without requiring either configuration to cease existing in the Library.

dependency_ladder.name: Persistence
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: \gamma = (x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_n) is persistent for O when each successive distinction remains resolvable.
dependency_ladder.explanation: The sequence index i represents abstract ordering only. It is not yet physical time. Persistence is the continuation of resolvable distinctions across an ordered chain.

dependency_ladder.name: Observer-relative coherence
dependency_ladder.explanation: Coherence can only be defined after observer-relative resolution has been established. It is therefore not an intrinsic property of a path alone. It is the relation between a path \gamma and an observer O: \mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O).

dependency_ladder.name: Observer-accessible reality
dependency_ladder.explanation: Accessibility is a relational subset of Library membership. A configuration outside A_O is not thereby removed from \mathcal{M}. Observer accessibility therefore does not create ontology, and inaccessibility does not constitute erasure.

dependency_ladder.name: Continuation space
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: \Omega(x)=\{\gamma\mid\gamma\text{ begins at }x\text{ and is a path contained in }\mathcal{M}\}
dependency_ladder.explanation: The full continuation space contains represented paths whether or not they survive the observer-relative coherence condition. Survivorship therefore filters accessible continuation rather than deleting alternatives from the underlying represented space.

dependency_ladder.name: Emergent regularity
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: Stable recurring transitions across an appropriate family of O-accessible paths may be represented by a derived relation L_O.
dependency_ladder.equation: L_O(x,y)=1 \iff x\to y\text{ is a stable recurring transition across an appropriate family of O-accessible paths}
dependency_ladder.explanation: Repeated survivorship can produce regularities that are describable in law-like terms. Such regularity is descriptive and derived. It is not an additional element of the axiom set and does not constitute a derivation of any particular physical law.

dependency_ladder.explanation: Once survivorship has restricted the represented continuation space, the next continuation is no longer selected from all represented paths indiscriminately. It is selected from the subset that remains coherent relative to O.

dependency_ladder.name: Navigation
dependency_ladder.explanation: Navigation is the traversal or selection of a continuation within the observer-relative coherent continuation space. It does not require the Library to generate a future. It is a continuation problem over already represented possibilities.

content.scope_boundary: The axiomatic floor ends before physical interpretation. It establishes a formal dependency chain from distinction to closure, from closure to persistent structures, from persistent structures to observer-relative resolution, from resolution to coherence, from coherence to accessibility and survivorship, and from restricted survivorship to coherent continuation. The next step is therefore not to add another foundational primitive, but to investigate what mathematical structure can be built on the coherent continuation space already defined.
content.handoff: The primer ends here. Subsequent NSFG research may now investigate the geometry, dynamics, topology, symbolic representation, or physical interpretation of coherent navigation without reintroducing the axiomatic floor.
